source.text: Kumārajīva, trans., Lotus Sutra, chapter 25, The Universal Gate of Avalokiteśvara (Taishō T262); the verses were added later by Jñānagupta and others

g01.heading: The Name Avalokiteśvara
g01.plain: Then Akṣayamati Bodhisattva rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha and asked: "World-Honored One, why is Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva called Avalokiteśvara?" The Buddha said: "Good son, if countless hundreds of thousands of millions of beings suffering all kinds of pain hear the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and call it single-mindedly, Avalokiteśvara at once perceives their voices and frees them all."
g01.commentary: Gwanseeum means "the one who perceives the sounds of the world." The meaning of the name, hearing the cries of suffering and rescuing, is the theme of the whole sutra.

g02.heading: Perils of Fire, Water and the Sea
g02.plain: Whoever holds the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva cannot be burned even if they enter a great fire, by the power of this bodhisattva. If swept away by a great flood, calling the name they reach shallow water at once. If people sail out to sea in search of treasure and a black wind drives their ship to the land of rākṣasas, and even one of them calls the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, they will all escape the peril of the rākṣasas. For this reason he is called Avalokiteśvara.
g02.commentary: Among the seven perils, these are fire, water, and the rākṣasas (wind).

g03.heading: Perils of Blades, Demons and Bonds
g03.plain: If someone about to be harmed calls the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, the swords and clubs held against them shatter to pieces and they escape. Even if yakṣas and rākṣasas filling the great trichiliocosm try to torment someone, when they hear the name of Avalokiteśvara being called they cannot even look at them with evil eyes, let alone harm them. Guilty or not, if someone bound hand and foot in cangue and chains calls the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, the bonds all break and they are freed.
g03.commentary: The perils of weapons, evil spirits and bonds.

g04.heading: The Peril of Bandits
g04.plain: When merchants carrying precious treasure pass along a dangerous road full of bandits, if one of them says, "Do not be afraid. Call the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva single-mindedly. This bodhisattva grants fearlessness to beings," and they all call out "Namo Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva," then because they called the name they escape at once. Akṣayamati, the majestic power of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is this lofty and great.
g04.commentary: This passage is the basis of the practice of reciting "Namo Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva." Namo means "I take refuge."

g05.heading: Freedom from Greed, Anger and Delusion
g05.plain: Beings full of desire, if they always keep Avalokiteśvara in mind and revere him, leave desire behind; those full of anger leave anger behind; those full of delusion leave delusion behind. Avalokiteśvara has such great power and brings so much benefit that beings should always keep him in their hearts.
g05.commentary: He frees beings not only from outer disasters but from the three poisons within: greed, anger and delusion.

g06.heading: Two Kinds of Wishes
g06.plain: If a woman who wishes for a son bows to and makes offerings to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, she will bear a son with merit and wisdom; if she wishes for a daughter, she will bear a graceful, lovely daughter who planted roots of virtue in past lives and is loved and respected by all. The merit of revering and bowing to Avalokiteśvara is never in vain, so all beings should hold his name.
g06.commentary: "Merit is never in vain" means that merit is never thrown away.

g07.heading: The Merit of Holding the Name
g07.plain: "Akṣayamati, if someone held the names of bodhisattvas as many as sixty-two hundred million Ganges sands and made offerings to them all their life of food, clothing, bedding and medicine, would their merit be great?" "Very great." "And if someone holds the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and bows and makes offerings even for a moment, the merit of the two is exactly equal and will not be exhausted in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas. Holding the name of Avalokiteśvara brings such measureless merit."
g07.commentary: It stresses that the name of Avalokiteśvara alone carries merit equal to the names of countless bodhisattvas.

g08.heading: The Thirty-Three Bodies (1)
g08.plain: Akṣayamati Bodhisattva asked: "How does Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva travel through this Sahā world and teach the Dharma to beings?" "Good son, to beings who can be saved by a Buddha's body, he appears in a Buddha's body and teaches the Dharma; to those who can be saved by the body of a pratyekabuddha, a śrāvaka, King Brahmā, Śakra, Īśvara, Maheśvara, a heavenly general or Vaiśravaṇa, he appears in that body and teaches the Dharma."
g08.commentary: Avalokiteśvara appears in thirty-three bodies, adapted to each person. "Universal Gate" means a gate open to everyone.

g09.heading: The Thirty-Three Bodies (2)
g09.plain: "To those who can be saved by the body of a minor king, an elder, a householder, an official or a brahmin; a monk, nun, layman or laywoman; a woman of any household; a boy or girl; a god, dragon, yakṣa or any of the eight kinds of beings, or a non-human; or a vajra-bearing guardian, he appears in that body and teaches the Dharma. Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva has achieved such merit, and in many forms he travels through many lands saving beings. So make offerings to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva single-mindedly. This bodhisattva grants fearlessness amid fear and urgent danger, which is why in the Sahā world everyone calls him 'the Giver of Fearlessness.'"
g09.commentary: From kings and officials to children and spirits, he reaches everyone in the form that suits them: this is the meaning of the Universal Gate.

g10.heading: The Offering of the Necklace
g10.plain: Akṣayamati Bodhisattva said, "I will now make an offering to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva," and took off his jeweled necklace worth hundreds of thousands of pieces of gold and offered it, but Avalokiteśvara would not accept it. "Kind one, out of compassion for us, please accept it." The Buddha too said, "Out of compassion for Akṣayamati Bodhisattva, the fourfold assembly and the eight kinds of beings, accept it." Then Avalokiteśvara accepted it, divided it in two, and offered one half to Śākyamuni Buddha and the other to the stupa of Prabhūtaratna Buddha. With such free spiritual power Avalokiteśvara travels through the Sahā world.
g10.commentary: Even the offering he receives he does not keep, but turns back to the Buddhas.

g11.heading: Verses · Question and Answer
g11.plain: Akṣayamati Bodhisattva asked in verse: "World-Honored One, endowed with wondrous marks, for what reason is this child of the Buddha called Avalokiteśvara?" The one endowed with wondrous marks answered in verse: "Listen to the practice of Avalokiteśvara, who responds rightly everywhere. His vast vows are as deep as the sea, beyond measure through many kalpas; serving a thousand million Buddhas he made great, pure vows. I will tell you briefly: hearing his name, seeing his form and keeping him in mind are not in vain; they end all suffering."
g11.commentary: From here the prose is sung again in five-character verses. This is the part most often chanted.

g12.heading: Verses · By the Power of Avalokiteśvara (1)
g12.plain: If someone with intent to harm pushes you into a great pit of fire, think of Avalokiteśvara's power and the pit of fire becomes a pond. Adrift on the sea amid perils of dragons, fish and demons, the waves cannot swallow you; pushed from the peak of Sumeru, you stay in the sky like the sun. Chased by evil people and falling from a diamond mountain, not a hair is harmed; surrounded by bandits with swords, they all turn compassionate. Facing death by royal punishment, the blade breaks into pieces; bound hand and foot in prison, you are suddenly freed; if curses and poisons are used to harm you, they return to the one who sent them.
g12.commentary: This is the part where "by the power of Avalokiteśvara," literally "thinking of that Avalokiteśvara's power," repeats again and again.

g13.heading: Verses · By the Power of Avalokiteśvara (2)
g13.plain: Meeting evil rākṣasas, poisonous dragons and demons, think of Avalokiteśvara's power and they dare not harm you; surrounded by fierce beasts with sharp teeth and claws, they flee far away. Though snakes and scorpions breathe poison like flames, at the sound they withdraw; though thunder and lightning strike and hail and rain pour down, they soon disperse. When beings fall into hardship and are tormented by measureless suffering, the wondrous power of Avalokiteśvara's wisdom rescues the world from suffering.
g13.commentary: It sings that he rescues from every suffering, naming even the dangers of nature and wild beasts.

g14.heading: Verses · Avalokiteśvara's Five Ways of Seeing
g14.plain: Endowed with spiritual powers and widely skilled in wisdom and means, there is no land in the ten directions where he does not appear. He gradually ends the evil paths of hells, hungry ghosts and animals, and the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness and death. True seeing, pure seeing, seeing with vast wisdom, seeing with compassion and seeing with loving-kindness: always long for them and look up to them. A spotless, pure light, the sun of wisdom breaks through all darkness, subdues the winds and fires of disaster, and shines over the whole world. His compassionate body is like the thunder of the precepts, his loving intent like a great cloud; he sends down the sweet rain of Dharma and quenches the flames of affliction.
g14.commentary: True seeing, pure seeing, vast-wisdom seeing, compassionate seeing and loving seeing are the five ways Avalokiteśvara looks upon beings.

g15.heading: Verses · Wondrous Sound Avalokiteśvara
g15.plain: Standing in court in a lawsuit or on a fearful battlefield, think of Avalokiteśvara's power and all enemies withdraw. Wondrous Sound, Avalokiteśvara, Pure Sound, Sound of the Tide: his voice surpasses every sound in the world, so keep him always in mind. Do not doubt, thought after thought. The pure sage Avalokiteśvara is a refuge in suffering and at the brink of death. Complete in every merit, he looks upon beings with compassionate eyes; his ocean of blessings is boundless. Therefore bow your head to him.
g15.commentary: "He looks upon beings with compassionate eyes; his ocean of blessings is boundless" is often recited in homage to Avalokiteśvara.

g16.heading: Conclusion
g16.plain: Then Dharaṇiṃdhara Bodhisattva rose and said: "World-Honored One, beings who hear of the free deeds of this Avalokiteśvara chapter and his spiritual power of manifesting through the Universal Gate will gain no small merit." When the Buddha taught this Universal Gate chapter, eighty-four thousand beings in the assembly all set their minds on unequalled, supreme awakening.
g16.commentary: "Unequalled" means "equal to that which has no equal": the awakening of a Buddha.

avalokitesvara.definition: The bodhisattva of compassion who perceives the sounds of the world and rescues beings from suffering. The same bodhisattva as Gwanjajae in the Heart Sutra.

namu.definition: "I take refuge, I rely on with my life." "Namo Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva" means taking refuge in Avalokiteśvara.
